text: All the initial influencers, I onboarded manually myself. I would jump on a call with each one of them so that they understood what Gamma represented, how to use the product.
speaker: Grant Lee
context: Lenny asks Grant about Gamma's influencer marketing strategy, which was a key growth lever for the company. Grant explains his hands-on approach to working with influencers and why targeting micro-influencers is more effective than working with large creators. He emphasizes the importance of authenticity in influencer partnerships rather than treating them as simple advertising placements.
text_ko: 초기 인플루언서들(influencers)은 모두 제가 직접 온보딩(onboarded)했어요. 한 분 한 분과 직접 통화하면서 Gamma가 어떤 가치를 제공하는지, 제품을 어떻게 사용하는지 이해하실 수 있게 설명해 드렸어요.
text_zh: 最开始那批影响者(influencer)，都是我一个一个亲自搞定的。我会跟每个人单独通电话，让他们明白Gamma是做什么的，产品怎么用。
text_es: Todos los primeros influencers los integré yo mismo manualmente. Me metía en llamadas con cada uno de ellos para que entendieran qué representaba Gamma, cómo usar el producto.
key_sentence: I would jump on a call with each one of them so that they understood what Gamma represented.
original_text: All the initial influencers, I onboarded manually myself. I would jump on a call with each one of them so that they understood what Gamma represented, how to use the product. You want to be able to have them tell you story but in their voice. I think a lot of people think influencer marketing and they'll think these big trendy creators, people that have a million followers. This is the wrong approach. You basically give them a script to read, immediately feels like an ad.

vocabulary.definition: The process of integrating a new employee, customer, or partner into an organization or system, ensuring they understand the necessary tools and culture.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech environments, onboarding is crucial for ensuring that new team members or clients can effectively engage with products or services from the outset.
vocabulary.nuance: While often used in a formal context, 'onboarded' can imply a more personal touch when it involves direct interaction, such as training or support.

vocabulary.definition: Individuals or entities that have the power to affect the purchasing decisions of others due to their authority, knowledge, position, or relationship with their audience.
vocabulary.businessContext: In marketing and social media, influencers are leveraged to promote products or services, as their endorsements can significantly impact brand visibility and consumer behavior.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can carry a positive connotation when referring to trusted figures, but may also imply a lack of authenticity if the influencer is perceived as solely profit-driven.

text: You're much better doing the hard thing, which is hard to scale, finding the thousands of micro influencers that have an audience where your product maybe is actually useful. People really trust what they say.
speaker: Grant Lee
context: Grant continues explaining his influencer marketing philosophy, contrasting his approach with traditional influencer marketing. He advocates for working with micro-influencers who have smaller but more engaged audiences that genuinely trust their recommendations. He describes how this strategy creates organic word-of-mouth growth that can spread rapidly through communities.
text_zh: 你最好还是做那些难做的事儿，虽然不好规模化，但要去找到那些有几千粉丝的小博主(micro influencers)，他们的受众可能真的会用你的产品。大家对这些人说的话是真的很信任的。
text_es: Es mucho mejor hacer lo difícil, que es difícil de escalar, encontrar a esos miles de micro influencers que tienen una audiencia donde tu producto realmente puede ser útil. La gente confía muchísimo en lo que dicen.
key_sentence: finding the thousands of micro influencers that have an audience where your product maybe is actually useful.
original_text: You're much better doing the hard thing, which is hard to scale, finding the thousands of micro influencers that have an audience where your product maybe is actually useful. People really trust what they say. That ends up becoming this wildfire that can spread really, really fast.

vocabulary.definition: To increase in size, amount, or capacity, often in a systematic way.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, scaling refers to the ability to grow operations or revenue without a corresponding increase in costs, often leveraging technology or processes.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'scale' often implies growth, it can also suggest the efficiency of that growth; it's important to differentiate between scaling and simply expanding.

vocabulary.definition: A group of individuals who consume content, products, or services, often defined by shared characteristics or interests.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, understanding the target audience is crucial for effective marketing strategies, product development, and customer engagement.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'audience' can imply a passive group; however, in modern marketing, it often refers to active participants who engage with brands and content.

vocabulary.definition: A firm belief in the reliability, truth, or ability of someone or something.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, trust is essential for building customer relationships, fostering brand loyalty, and encouraging repeat purchases.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'trust' is a fundamental aspect of relationships, it can be fragile and requires consistent effort to maintain, especially in competitive markets.

text: We would have an idea in the morning, come up with some sort of functional prototype, recruit a bunch of people that are legitimately good prospective users, but have zero skin in the game, ship fast so people can start playing with it.
speaker: Grant Lee
context: Lenny asks Grant about Gamma's experimental approach to product development. Grant describes their rapid prototyping and user testing workflow, where they can go from idea to user feedback within a single day. This process involves recruiting unbiased potential users to test prototypes and observe their real interactions with the product, allowing the team to identify usability issues quickly.
text_ko: 아침에 아이디어가 떠오르면 그날 바로 대충 작동하는 프로토타입(functional prototype)을 만들고, 진짜로 적합한 잠재 사용자들(prospective users)을 여러 명 모집했어요. 다만 그분들은 실제로는 이해관계(skin in the game)가 전혀 없었고요. 사람들이 바로 써볼 수 있게 빠르게 출시했어요.
text_zh: 我们早上有个想法，就赶紧做个能用的原型出来，然后找一帮真正会用这个产品的人——但是跟我们没有利益关系的那种，快速上线让大家试用。
text_es: Teníamos una idea por la mañana, armábamos algún tipo de prototipo funcional, conseguíamos un grupo de gente que fueran buenos usuarios potenciales de verdad, pero que no tuvieran nada que ver con el proyecto, y lanzábamos rápido para que la gente empezara a probarlo.
key_sentence: ship fast so people can start playing with it.
original_text: We would have an idea in the morning, come up with some sort of functional prototype, recruit a bunch of people that are legitimately good prospective users, but have zero skin in the game, ship fast so people can start playing with it. In the afternoon, we're already running pretty full scale experiment. You start actually hearing other people describe their usage of the product. We can also watch them struggle.

vocabulary.definition: A functional prototype is an early model of a product that demonstrates its core features and functionality, allowing for testing and feedback before full-scale production.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, functional prototypes are essential for validating ideas, gathering user feedback, and iterating on product design in a cost-effective manner.
vocabulary.nuance: While a functional prototype is not the final product, it should be sufficiently developed to provide meaningful insights and user experiences.

vocabulary.definition: Prospective users are individuals or groups who are potential customers or end-users of a product or service, often identified during market research.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startup settings, understanding the needs and behaviors of prospective users is crucial for product development and marketing strategies.
vocabulary.nuance: The term implies a forward-looking perspective, focusing on individuals who have not yet engaged with the product but are likely to do so.

vocabulary.definition: Having skin in the game means having a personal stake or investment in a project or venture, which aligns one's interests with its success.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, stakeholders with skin in the game are often more motivated to contribute to the success of a project, as their own resources or reputation are on the line.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase often carries a connotation of accountability and commitment, suggesting that those without skin in the game may lack the same level of investment or concern.

text: I think most people today are probably familiar with founder-led sales, which is still very, very important. I think before you hire your first salesperson or AE, it's great for the founder to understand what it takes.
speaker: Grant Lee
context: Grant explains the concept of founder-led marketing by drawing parallels to founder-led sales. He argues that just as founders should understand sales before hiring salespeople, they should also understand marketing and storytelling before delegating these functions. This hands-on approach helps founders develop better narratives and maintain higher standards when working with marketing professionals or influencers.
text_ko: 요즘 대부분 사람들은 창업자 주도 영업(founder-led sales)에 익숙하실 거예요. 첫 영업사원이나 AE(Account Executive)를 채용하기 전에 창업자가 직접 그 일이 어떤 건지, 무엇이 필요한지 잘 파악해 두는 게 좋아요.
text_zh: 我觉得现在大部分人应该都知道创始人亲自做销售这回事，这个还是非常非常重要的。我觉得在你招第一个销售或者客户经理(AE)之前，创始人自己先搞明白这里面的门道是很有必要的。
text_es: Creo que la mayoría de la gente hoy en día ya conoce las ventas lideradas por el fundador (founder-led sales), que siguen siendo súper importantes. Me parece que antes de contratar a tu primer vendedor o AE (account executive), está padrísimo que el fundador entienda lo que se necesita.
key_sentence: it's great for the founder to understand what it takes.
original_text: I think most people today are probably familiar with founder-led sales, which is still very, very important. I think before you hire your first salesperson or AE, it's great for the founder to understand what it takes. And they're going to craft the right narrative, the right story.

vocabulary.definition: Referring to a business or initiative that is primarily directed and managed by its founder, often emphasizing their vision and leadership.
vocabulary.businessContext: In startup environments, founder-led sales are crucial as they leverage the founder's deep understanding of the product and market to drive initial sales efforts.
vocabulary.nuance: This term often implies a hands-on approach and can suggest a strong personal investment from the founder in the company's success.

vocabulary.definition: To grasp the meaning, significance, or nature of something, often involving comprehension of complex concepts.
vocabulary.businessContext: In a business context, understanding market dynamics, customer needs, and operational processes is essential for effective decision-making and strategy formulation.
vocabulary.nuance: This term conveys a depth of knowledge that goes beyond superficial awareness, indicating a thorough comprehension of the subject matter.

vocabulary.definition: Of great significance or value; having a major effect on outcomes or decisions.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business discussions, identifying important factors or metrics is crucial for prioritizing actions and aligning team efforts towards strategic goals.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'important' suggests a high level of significance, it can be subjective and context-dependent, varying in weight based on the situation.

vocabulary.definition: An individual whose primary role is to sell products or services, often engaging directly with customers to facilitate transactions.
vocabulary.businessContext: Salespersons are vital in driving revenue for businesses, as they build relationships with clients and identify opportunities for sales growth.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply a range of skills from persuasive communication to technical knowledge, and is often associated with a proactive approach to customer engagement.

text: I think there's that saying where obviously if you can have that clarity, that's super important. And most people will try to get super creative with their copywriting, but that's not usually the right way to break through and communicate something.
speaker: Grant Lee
context: Grant discusses the importance of clear communication in founder-led marketing. He references the principle of prioritizing clarity over creativity in copywriting, suggesting that founders should focus on being understood rather than being clever. This advice comes in the context of explaining how founders can develop better marketing skills by practicing copywriting themselves.
text_ko: 사실 명확함을 가질 수 있다면 그게 정말 중요하다고들 해요. 대부분 사람들은 카피라이팅(copywriting)을 엄청 창의적으로 하려고 하는데, 보통 그게 주목을 끌거나 메시지를 제대로 전달하는 올바른 방법은 아니에요.
text_zh: 我觉得有句话说得对，如果你能把话说清楚，这点特别重要。很多人写文案的时候总想搞得特别有创意，但这通常不是突破和沟通的正确方式。
text_es: Creo que hay un dicho que dice que si puedes ser claro, eso es súper importante. Y la mayoría de la gente trata de ponerse súper creativa con sus textos, pero normalmente esa no es la forma correcta de conectar y comunicar algo.
key_sentence: Clarity is super important to break through and communicate effectively in copywriting.
original_text: I think there's that saying where obviously if you can have that clarity, that's super important. And most people will try to get super creative with their copywriting, but that's not usually the right way to break through and communicate something. So how do you improve your own copywriting?

vocabulary.definition: The quality of being clear and easy to understand; the absence of ambiguity.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, clarity is essential for effective communication, ensuring that messages are understood by all stakeholders and reducing the risk of misunderstandings.
vocabulary.nuance: Clarity often implies a straightforward approach, which is preferred in professional settings to avoid confusion.

vocabulary.definition: To convey information or express thoughts and feelings to others through speaking, writing, or other means.
vocabulary.businessContext: Effective communication is vital in business for collaboration, negotiation, and relationship-building among teams and clients.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'communicate' can refer to any form of information exchange, in a business context, it often emphasizes clarity and purpose.

vocabulary.definition: The act of writing text for advertising or marketing purposes, aimed at persuading an audience to take action.
vocabulary.businessContext: In marketing and advertising, effective copywriting is crucial for creating compelling messages that engage consumers and drive sales.
vocabulary.nuance: While creativity is valued in copywriting, it is important to maintain clarity and focus on the intended message to achieve desired outcomes.

text: I think what I've learned is, even for LinkedIn versus Twitter, the audiences want different things. And so you almost have to then have different tones of voices or even nuggets or sharing.
speaker: Grant Lee
context: Grant shares his approach to social media marketing across different platforms. He explains how he learned that LinkedIn and Twitter audiences have different preferences and expectations, requiring tailored content strategies for each platform. This insight led him to develop platform-specific approaches rather than simply cross-posting the same content everywhere.
text_ko: 제가 배운 건, LinkedIn이든 Twitter든 플랫폼마다 청중이 원하는 게 다르다는 거예요. 그래서 거의 다른 톤(tone of voice)을 쓰거나, 심지어 공유하는 핵심 콘텐츠(nuggets)까지 달리해야 해요.
text_zh: 我觉得我学到的是，LinkedIn和Twitter(推特)上的用户群体想要的东西完全不一样。所以你基本上得用不同的语调，甚至分享不同类型的内容。
text_es: Creo que lo que he aprendido es que, incluso entre LinkedIn y Twitter, la gente quiere cosas diferentes. Entonces casi que tienes que cambiar tu tono de voz o hasta el tipo de contenido que compartes.
original_text: I think what I've learned is, even for LinkedIn versus Twitter, the audiences want different things. And so you almost have to then have different tones of voices or even nuggets or sharing. For me, I invested much more in LinkedIn early on just because it felt a little bit more natural for me. And then over time I said, 'Okay, well I'm going to start packaging certain content for Twitter that's actually different than what I would post on LinkedIn.'

vocabulary.definition: Groups of individuals who consume or engage with content, products, or services.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, understanding different audiences is crucial for tailoring marketing strategies and communication to meet their specific needs and preferences.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often implies a segmentation of consumers based on demographics, interests, or behaviors, highlighting the importance of targeted messaging.

vocabulary.definition: The distinctive way in which a message is conveyed, reflecting the personality and attitude of the communicator.
vocabulary.businessContext: In branding and marketing, varying tones of voice can help establish a connection with different audiences, influencing how messages are perceived and received.
vocabulary.nuance: Choosing the appropriate tone of voice is essential for aligning with brand identity and audience expectations; a mismatch can lead to misunderstandings.
